title: Length-Weight Relationship Analysis
text:
This practical exercise demonstrates the analysis of length-weight relationships in fish, using a case study of Snappers (Family Lutjanidae) from Tanzanian coastal waters. Snappers are important demersal fish in Tanzania’s fisheries and exhibit approximately isometric growth, meaning their body shape remains relatively constant as they grow.
The length-weight relationship is described by the equation:
\[W = a \times L^b\]
where:

W = Weight (in grams)
L = Length (in centimeters)
a = Intercept (related to body shape/condition)
b = Slope (scaling exponent, typically ~3 for isometric growth)

Snappers are important demersal fish in Tanzania’s fisheries and exhibit approximately isometric growth, meaning their body shape remains relatively constant as they grow.
The length-weight relationship is described by the equation:
\[W = a \times L^b\]

title: Length-Weight Relationship Analysis
text:
Objectives

Analyze length-weight data from a Tanzanian marine fish species
Fit a linear regression model to log-transformed data
Visualize the relationship using ggplot2
Extract parameter estimates (a and b)
Interpret biological significance of the results

title: Length-Weight Relationship Analysis
text:
Data Generation
We’ll create realistic length-weight data for Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) caught in Tanzanian waters. For isometric growth, we expect b ≈ 3.

# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyplots)


# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(642)

# Generate length-weight data for Red Snapper (isometric growth)
# Parameters based on typical Tanzanian snapper populations

n_samples <- 80

lw_data <- tibble(
  # Length in cm (realistic range for snappers: 15-65 cm)
  length_cm = rnorm(n_samples, mean = 38, sd = 12) %>% 
    pmax(15) %>% pmin(65),  # Constrain to realistic range
  
  # Weight in grams, calculated from isometric relationship
  # For snappers: W = 0.015 * L^3.02 (approximately isometric)
  weight_g = 0.015 * (length_cm ^ 3.02) + rnorm(n_samples, mean = 0, sd = 15)
) %>%
  # Ensure positive weights
  filter(weight_g > 0) %>%
  arrange(length_cm)

title: Length-Weight Relationship Analysis
text:
Linear Regression Analysis
To extract the parameters a and b, we fit a linear model to the log-transformed equation:

lw_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = length_cm, y = weight_g)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8, color = "#2E86AB") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, formula = y ~ poly(x, 3), color = "#A23B72", size = 1) +
  # ggpubr::stat_regline_equation() +
  labs(
    title = "Length-Weight Scatter Plot",
    x = "Length (cm)",
    y = "Weight (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold")
  )








\[\log(W) = \log(a) + b \times \log(L)\]
This transforms the power-law relationship into a linear relationship suitable for regression analysis.

lw_log = lw_data |> 
  mutate(log_length = log(length_cm),
        log_weight = log(weight_g)) 

fit_lw = lm(log_weight ~ log_length, data = lw_log) # model fitting

y_intercept = coef(fit_lw)[1]
slope = coef(fit_lw)[2]

# Calculating values for a

# log(a) = y_intercept => a = exp(y_intercept)

a = exp(y_intercept) # 0.01080354 
b = slope  # 3.110061


lw_log  |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log_length, y = log_weight)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, color = "#2E86AB") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, formula = y ~ x, color = "#A23B72", size = 1) +
  ggpubr::stat_regline_equation() +
  labs(
    title = "Length-Weight Scatter Plot",
    x = "Log of Length",
    y = "Log of Weight"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold")
  )

title: Length-Weight Relationship Analysis
text:
Condition Factor Analysis
The condition factor (K or CF) is a measure of the fish’s health and robustness. It is calculated as:
\[K = \frac{W}{L^b} \times 100\]
where:

W = Weight (in grams)
L = Length (in centimeters)
b = Slope from the length-weight equation (scaling exponent)

The condition factor indicates whether a fish is in good condition (higher values) or poor condition (lower values) relative to its size.

# Calculate condition factor for each fish
k_data <- lw_data %>%
  mutate(
    condition_factor = (weight_g / (length_cm ^ slope)) * 100,
    # Also calculate relative condition factor (K_rel)
    # Expected weight based on regression
    expected_weight = a * (length_cm ^ slope),
    relative_condition = (weight_g / expected_weight) * 100
  )

    method = "loess",

title: Length-Weight Relationship Analysis
text:
Summary and Interpretation
The analysis demonstrates several key findings:

Growth Pattern: The slope value (b = 3.11) indicates that the Red Snapper exhibits isometric growth. With b ≈ 3, the fish maintains proportional body shape as it grows, meaning weight increases approximately with the cube of length.
Model Fit: The R² value of 0.9947 indicates that 99.5% of the variation in weight is explained by length. This is typical for biological length-weight relationships.
Parameter Estimates:

a = 0.010804 - This relates to the body condition and shape of the fish
b = 3.1101 - This scaling exponent is close to 3, confirming isometric growth

Fisheries Application: This relationship allows fisheries managers and researchers to:

Estimate biomass from length measurements alone
Monitor changes in population condition over time
Assess growth rates and health status
Convert between length and weight data in stock assessments

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
\[SSB = \frac{P_0 \times A}{R \times S \times F}\]
Where: - SSB = Spawning stock biomass - \(P_0\) = Daily egg production per unit area - \(A\) = Spawning area - \(R\) = Sex ratio (proportion female) - \(S\) = Spawning fraction (proportion spawning per day) - \(F\) = Batch fecundity (eggs per spawning female)

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
Question 1: Basic Calculation
A sardine spawning survey in Tanzanian coastal waters collected the following data:

Daily egg production per unit area (\(P_0\)) = 450 eggs/m²/day
Spawning area (\(A\)) = 5,000 km²
Sex ratio (\(R\)) = 0.52 (52% female)
Spawning fraction (\(S\)) = 0.35 (35% spawn per day)
Batch fecundity (\(F\)) = 12,000 eggs/female

Calculate the spawning stock biomass (SSB).

Answer:
First, convert spawning area to m²: \[A = 5,000 \text{ km}^2 = 5,000 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^2 = 5 \times 10^9 \text{ m}^2\]
Apply DEPM formula: \[SSB = \frac{450 \times 5 \times 10^9}{0.52 \times 0.35 \times 12,000}\]
\[SSB = \frac{2.25 \times 10^{12}}{2,184} = 1.03 \times 10^9 \text{ eggs}\]
Converting to biomass (sardine eggs ~0.75 mg = 0.00075 g per egg): \[1.03 \times 10^9 \text{ eggs} \times 0.00075 \text{ g/egg} = 7.73 \times 10^8 \text{ g}\]
Convert to tonnes (1 tonne = \(10^6\) g): \[\frac{7.73 \times 10^8 \text{ g}}{10^6 \text{ g/tonne}} = 773 \text{ tonnes}\]
\[SSB \approx 773 \text{ tonnes}\]

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
Question 2: Parameter Interpretation
Explain what each parameter in the DEPM formula represents and why it is important for SSB estimation.

Answer:

\(P_0\) (Daily Egg Production): Measures spawning intensity in the survey area. Higher \(P_0\) indicates active spawning; reflects reproductive output per unit spawning habitat.
\(A\) (Spawning Area): Geographic extent of the spawning ground. Larger area = greater total egg production. Accurate delineation is critical.
\(R\) (Sex Ratio): Only females produce eggs. Must adjust for proportion of females in spawning population. Typically 0.48-0.52 depending on species.
\(S\) (Spawning Fraction): Not all females spawn on a given day. Varies by species and environmental conditions. Lower \(S\) = smaller daily fraction of stock spawning.
\(F\) (Batch Fecundity): Individual female reproductive capacity. Higher \(F\) = fewer females needed to produce observed eggs. Critical parameter often determined from histological analysis.

Importance: Each parameter affects SSB inversely or directly. Small errors in any parameter compound to large SSB estimation errors.

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
Question 3: Sensitivity Analysis
If spawning fraction (\(S\)) decreases from 0.40 to 0.25 due to poor environmental conditions, how does this affect SSB estimates? What does this imply biologically?

Answer:
Effect on SSB:
With \(S = 0.40\): Denominator = \(0.52 \times 0.40 \times 12,000 = 2,496\)
With \(S = 0.25\): Denominator = \(0.52 \times 0.25 \times 12,000 = 1,560\)
\[\frac{\text{SSB}_{new}}{\text{SSB}_{old}} = \frac{2,496}{1,560} = 1.60\]
SSB increases by 60% for same number of observed eggs.
Biological Implication:
If fewer females spawn per day (\(S\) decreases), a larger total stock is required to produce the observed daily egg production. This indicates:

Reduced spawning activity per individual female
Possible physiological stress (food scarcity, temperature extremes, pollution)
Recruitment failure or poor condition of females
Need for management intervention (reduced fishing pressure)

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
Question 4: Data Collection Problem
A researcher estimates spawning stock biomass using DEPM but realizes the sex ratio in the spawning population differs from the population overall. How would this bias SSB estimates?

Answer:
Scenario 1: Actual \(R\) > Assumed \(R\)
If more females spawn than assumed: - Denominator is underestimated - SSB estimates are inflated (overestimate of true stock) - Result: More liberal catch recommendations (dangerous)
Scenario 2: Actual \(R\) < Assumed \(R\)
If fewer females spawn than assumed: - Denominator is overestimated - SSB estimates are deflated (underestimate of true stock) - Result: More conservative catch recommendations (safer)
Why This Matters:
Sex ratio bias directly affects SSB by factor of (assumed \(R\) / actual \(R\)). A 10% error in sex ratio causes ~10% error in SSB.
Solution: - Sample spawning ground directly - Use separate sex ratio estimates from spawning area - Conduct sensitivity analysis on \(R\) uncertainty

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
Question 5: Application Question
A small pelagic fishery in Zanzibar wants to set catch limits based on SSB estimates from DEPM. What assumptions must be met for this method to be reliable?

Answer:
Biological Assumptions:

Pelagic eggs: Eggs develop in water column (accessible to sampling). Not suitable for demersal or adhesive eggs.
Defined spawning area: Spawning concentrated in identifiable, accessible location. Not dispersed throughout stock range.
Synchronous spawning: Most females spawn within defined period (season/month).
Steady-state stock: Population not experiencing catastrophic recruitment failure or exceptional year-classes.

Data Assumptions:

Accurate fecundity (\(F\)): Must be determined from gonad analysis of spawning females. Not from historical literature.
Accurate sex ratio (\(R\)): Sampled directly from spawning grounds, not from general population.
Accurate spawning fraction (\(S\)): Requires histological analysis or mark-recapture on spawning ground.
Representative \(P_0\) sampling: Survey must cover entire spawning area, account for spatial patchiness.

Oceanographic Assumptions:

Negligible egg mortality: Assumes eggs survive until next sampling occasion (typically <24 hours).
No egg advection: Spawned eggs remain in survey area (weak currents).

If assumptions violated:

SSB estimates become unreliable
Catch recommendations may be inappropriate
Use sensitivity analysis or combine with other methods (acoustic, VPA, CPUE)

Recommendation: Use DEPM combined with 1-2 other methods for cross-validation.

title: Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM) - Sample Questions
text:
Question 7: Real Data Problem
Given the following data from a Zanzibar anchovy spawning survey:

Survey area: 2,500 km²
Average daily egg production: 320 eggs/m²
Sex ratio: 0.50
Spawning fraction: 0.30
Batch fecundity: 8,500 eggs/female
Survey duration: 5 days
Total catch during survey: 150 tonnes

Calculate:

Spawning stock biomass
Exploitation rate (Catch/SSB)
Is this sustainable? (Assume target exploitation rate = 10%)


Answer:
a) Calculate SSB:
\[SSB = \frac{320 \times 2,500 \times 10^6}{0.50 \times 0.30 \times 8,500}\]
\[SSB = \frac{8 \times 10^{11}}{1,275} = 6.27 \times 10^8 \text{ eggs}\]
Converting to biomass (anchovy eggs ~0.75 mg per egg): \[6.27 \times 10^8 \text{ eggs} \times 0.00075 \text{ g/egg} = 4.70 \times 10^8 \text{ g} = 470 \text{ tonnes}\]
SSB = 470 tonnes
b) Exploitation Rate:
\[E = \frac{\text{Catch}}{\text{SSB}} = \frac{150}{470} = 0.319 = 31.9\%\]
c) Sustainability Assessment:

Current exploitation: 31.9%
Target exploitation: 10%
Conclusion: Stock is overexploited at current fishing pressure. Catch should be reduced to ~47 tonnes to meet the 10% target exploitation rate
This indicates unsustainable harvest levels and need for management intervention

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Define a unit stock and explain the key characteristics that distinguish one unit stock from another.


A unit stock is a population of fish (single or multiple species) grouped together for assessment and management purposes that shares a common gene pool and occupies a defined geographical area.
Key characteristics: - Common gene pool – Can interbreed and maintain genetic continuity - Defined geographic area – Specific distribution boundaries and habitat - Similar life history traits – Comparable growth, reproduction, and mortality rates - Common fishing pressures – Subject to same fisheries and exploitation patterns - Managed as single entity – Can be independently managed and assessed
Significance: Unit stocks allow management of complex multispecies tropical fisheries by dividing populations into manageable units for assessment and conservation.





You are tasked with determining whether yellowfin tuna in the Indian Ocean constitute one stock or multiple unit stocks. What methods would you use, and what data would you collect?


Methods for stock determination:

Genetic analysis – DNA markers, microsatellites to assess gene flow and population structure
Morphometric analysis – Vertebrae counts, scale patterns, size-at-age differences
Parasitology – Parasite species/intensity indicating isolation
Otolith microchemistry – Chemical signatures reflecting spawning area origin
Tagging studies – Track movements and migration patterns

Data to collect: - Tissue samples from throughout Indian Ocean - Spawning location records (time, area, temperature) - Growth rates at different locations - Catch composition and fishing effort data - Environmental data (temperature, currents, productivity)
Expected outcomes: Multiple stocks likely exist (e.g., eastern, western Indian Ocean; seasonal variations)





A lake contains an estimated 50,000 tilapia. A survey found spawning occurring in two separate locations with different substrate types. Genetic analysis shows 85% within-population similarity but only 42% between-population similarity. Should these be managed as one or two unit stocks?


Analysis: - Within-population similarity (85%) indicates relatively homogeneous genetics - Between-population similarity (42%) suggests significant differentiation and limited gene flow - Separate spawning locations with different habitats indicate ecological separation
Recommendation: Manage as TWO UNIT STOCKS
Rationale: - Low between-population genetic similarity (<50%) indicates reproductive isolation - Separate spawning habitats with different substrates suggest adapted populations - Independent management prevents mixing strategies and allows location-specific interventions - May have different growth rates, maturity ages, vulnerability to fishing





Discuss the importance of properly identifying and delineating unit stocks for fisheries management in Tanzania’s coastal waters. Include examples of straddling and highly migratory species.


Importance of unit stock identification:

Accurate Assessment – Proper stock delineation ensures abundance estimates reflect actual population boundaries, not artificial divisions
Sustainable Harvesting – Prevents overfishing by matching catch limits to correct population size. Mixing stocks artificially inflates perceived population
Management Independence – Allows location-specific regulations (closed seasons, gear restrictions) suited to each stock’s dynamics
International Coordination – Critical for stocks crossing borders (EEZ boundaries)

Tanzanian Examples:
Straddling Species: - Yellowfin tuna – Exists in both Tanzania’s EEZ and high seas; managed by IOTC - Swordfish – Distributed across multiple EEZs; requires transboundary agreements - Kingfish – Moves between Tanzanian and Kenyan waters seasonally
Highly Migratory Species: - Bigeye tuna – Oceanic distribution throughout Indian Ocean - Albacore – Annual migrations across thousands of kilometers
Management Challenges: - Must coordinate with IOTC and neighboring countries - Catch limits set at regional level may not reflect Tanzania’s specific fishing pressure - Stock mixing complicates assessment of Tanzania’s impact on global stocks
Recommendation: Establish Tanzania-specific monitoring for shared stocks; coordinate assessment data with regional management bodies

Define a unit stock and explain the key characteristics that distinguish one unit stock from another.


A unit stock is a population of fish (single or multiple species) grouped together for assessment and management purposes that shares a common gene pool and occupies a defined geographical area.
Key characteristics: - Common gene pool – Can interbreed and maintain genetic continuity - Defined geographic area – Specific distribution boundaries and habitat - Similar life history traits – Comparable growth, reproduction, and mortality rates - Common fishing pressures – Subject to same fisheries and exploitation patterns - Managed as single entity – Can be independently managed and assessed
Significance: Unit stocks allow management of complex multispecies tropical fisheries by dividing populations into manageable units for assessment and conservation.

A lake contains an estimated 50,000 tilapia. A survey found spawning occurring in two separate locations with different substrate types. Genetic analysis shows 85% within-population similarity but only 42% between-population similarity. Should these be managed as one or two unit stocks?


Analysis: - Within-population similarity (85%) indicates relatively homogeneous genetics - Between-population similarity (42%) suggests significant differentiation and limited gene flow - Separate spawning locations with different habitats indicate ecological separation
Recommendation: Manage as TWO UNIT STOCKS
Rationale: - Low between-population genetic similarity (<50%) indicates reproductive isolation - Separate spawning habitats with different substrates suggest adapted populations - Independent management prevents mixing strategies and allows location-specific interventions - May have different growth rates, maturity ages, vulnerability to fishing

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Discuss the importance of properly identifying and delineating unit stocks for fisheries management in Tanzania’s coastal waters. Include examples of straddling and highly migratory species.


Importance of unit stock identification:

Accurate Assessment – Proper stock delineation ensures abundance estimates reflect actual population boundaries, not artificial divisions
Sustainable Harvesting – Prevents overfishing by matching catch limits to correct population size. Mixing stocks artificially inflates perceived population
Management Independence – Allows location-specific regulations (closed seasons, gear restrictions) suited to each stock’s dynamics
International Coordination – Critical for stocks crossing borders (EEZ boundaries)

Tanzanian Examples:
Straddling Species: - Yellowfin tuna – Exists in both Tanzania’s EEZ and high seas; managed by IOTC - Swordfish – Distributed across multiple EEZs; requires transboundary agreements - Kingfish – Moves between Tanzanian and Kenyan waters seasonally
Highly Migratory Species: - Bigeye tuna – Oceanic distribution throughout Indian Ocean - Albacore – Annual migrations across thousands of kilometers
Management Challenges: - Must coordinate with IOTC and neighboring countries - Catch limits set at regional level may not reflect Tanzania’s specific fishing pressure - Stock mixing complicates assessment of Tanzania’s impact on global stocks
Recommendation: Establish Tanzania-specific monitoring for shared stocks; coordinate assessment data with regional management bodies

Model Answer:

Disadvantages: - High cost and equipment requirements - Limited temporal coverage - Species/habitat specific (not universally applicable) - Logistically demanding

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Question 2.5 (CPUE Standardization)
A longline fishery for yellowfin tuna in Tanzanian waters has 10 years of catch data. Raw CPUE (catch/hooks) shows declining trend. However, you notice: - Vessel technology improved (GPS, sonar, better refrigeration) - Fishing season shifted from Jan-June to Mar-August - Number of vessels increased from 5 to 25
How would you standardize CPUE to account for these factors? What statistical method would you use?

Model Answer:
Standardization Approach: Generalized Linear Model (GLM)
Model specification: \[\ln(\text{CPUE}) = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{Year} + \beta_2 \text{Season} + \beta_3 \text{Vessel\_Age} + \beta_4 \text{Technology} + \varepsilon\]
Factors to include: 1. Year – Captures stock abundance trend (primary variable of interest) 2. Season – Accounts for seasonal availability/migration (categorical: Jan-Jun vs Mar-Aug) 3. Vessel size/class – Standardize effort across different vessel types 4. Technology level – Include GPS, sonar availability as binary factors 5. Fishing ground – If spatial data available, include location
Alternative: Generalized Additive Model (GAM) - More flexible for non-linear relationships - Better captures smoothed trends over time - Allows interaction between factors
Interpretation: - β₁ (Year coefficient) = annual change in standardized CPUE - Negative β₁ = declining stock abundance (accounting for confounding factors) - Compare to raw CPUE to assess technology/behavior bias
Expected result: Standardized CPUE may show less decline (or even slight recovery) compared to raw CPUE, indicating technology improvements masked actual stock status

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Question 3.1 (Terminology)
Define and provide examples for each migration category:

Diadromous fish – subcategories: anadromous, catadromous, amphidromous
Potamodromous fish
Oceanodromous fish


Model Answer:
a) Diadromous – Migrate between marine and freshwater environments

Anadromous (born in freshwater, spawn in freshwater)

Examples: Salmon, sea trout, shad
Spawn in rivers, juveniles migrate to ocean, adults return to spawn
High investment in single spawning event

Catadromous (born in marine, spawn in marine)

Examples: Freshwater eel, milkfish
Spend most life in freshwater, migrate to sea to spawn

Amphidromous (no spawning migration)

Examples: Mullet, tilapia (some), ten-pounder
Larvae spawned in marine environment drift to freshwater
Settle and grow in freshwater as juveniles
No return migration to spawn


b) Potamodromous – Migrate wholly within freshwater

Examples: Trout, bream, coregonids (whitefish), Nile tilapia
Landlocked species with seasonal migrations
Migrate for spawning, feeding, or seasonal redistribution
Often triggered by water level/temperature changes

c) Oceanodromous – Migrate wholly within ocean

Examples: Cod, herring, capelin, yellowfin tuna, mackerel
Long-distance oceanic migrations (thousands of km)
Spawning grounds separate from feeding grounds
Highly migratory species (tuna, billfish) may cross ocean basins

Stock Assessment Implications: - Diadromous species require collaborative management between freshwater/marine authorities - Potamodromous species vulnerable to river barriers and freshwater habitat degradation - Oceanodromous species require international coordination (regional fisheries bodies like IOTC)

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Question 3.2 (Acoustic Surveys - Theory)
Explain the principle of acoustic fish detection. Include: a) How echo sounders detect fish b) Why frequency selection matters c) The concept of target strength

Model Answer:
a) Echo sounder principle:

Signal transmission – Transducer emits brief sound pulse into water
Reflection – Sound reflects off objects different in density from water (fish swim bladders)
Echo return – Reflected sound returns to receiver
Distance calculation – Time delay × sound speed = distance to object
Amplitude analysis – Echo strength indicates fish size/density

b) Frequency selection:

High frequency (>200 kHz) – Short wavelength, can detect plankton and small fish
Lower frequency (<200 kHz) – Penetrates deeper, detects larger fish, better range
Trade-off – Higher frequency = better resolution but shorter range
Species considerations – Small pelagics use 38-200 kHz; demersal surveys use 10-18 kHz

Example: - Sardine/anchovy surveys: 38-120 kHz (schools near surface, need resolution) - Demersal surveys: 10-18 kHz (greater depth penetration required)
c) Target Strength (TS):
\[TS = 20 \log_{10}(L) + b_{20}\]

TS = Acoustic reflectivity (dB)
L = Fish length (cm)
\(b_{20}\) = Species-specific constant (typically −70 to −72 dB)

Interpretation: - Larger fish have stronger target strength - Allows size discrimination from acoustic returns - Critical for converting acoustic backscatter to abundance estimates
Example values: - Herring (20 cm): TS ≈ -40 dB - Sardine (12 cm): TS ≈ -50 dB - Anchovy (10 cm): TS ≈ -55 dB

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Question 4.1 (Conceptual)
Define the length-weight relationship (LWR). Explain: a) The biological meaning of the equation \(W = aL^b\) b) What isometric growth means c) Why LWR is important in fisheries management

Model Answer:
a) LWR equation: \(W = aL^b\)

W = Weight (g or kg)
L = Length (cm or mm)
a = Condition coefficient (species and environment specific)
b = Growth exponent (allometric coefficient)

Biological interpretation: - Describes how weight scales with length across population - \(b = 3\) predicts isometric growth (weight increases with L³) - \(b ≠ 3\) indicates allometric growth (disproportionate weight-to-length ratio) - Typically fits power-law relationship due to 3D body structure
b) Isometric growth (\(b = 3\)):

Fish maintains constant body shape and density as it grows
Weight ∝ Length³ (volume relationship)
Example: Red snapper with b = 3.02

Allometric growth (\(b ≠ 3\)): - b > 3: Fish becomes proportionally heavier with growth (“deepening body”) - b < 3: Fish becomes proportionally lighter with growth (“thinning body”) - May reflect seasonal changes, sexual maturity, environmental conditions
c) Importance in fisheries management:

Condition monitoring – Deviation from species-specific LWR indicates health/nutrition
Stock assessment – Convert length data to biomass estimates
Population dynamics – Combine with age-length keys for cohort analysis
Size regulations – Establish minimum/maximum size limits based on weight-length trade-offs
Market standards – Determine fish value/quality
Climate impacts – Changes in slope/intercept may reflect environmental stress

Question 4.2 (Calculation)
Red snapper length-weight data collected from Tanzanian coastal waters show: - Sample size: 80 fish - Length range: 10-55 cm - Power-law regression: \(\ln(W) = -2.45 + 3.02 \times \ln(L)\) (R² = 0.94)
Calculate: a) Parameter a and b b) Expected weight at L = 30 cm and L = 50 cm c) Condition factor K at each length d) Assess growth pattern (isometric or allometric)

Model Answer:
a) Extract parameters from regression:
From \(\ln(W) = -2.45 + 3.02 \times \ln(L)\):

\(\ln(a) = -2.45\), therefore a = e^{-2.45} = 0.086
b = 3.02

Equation: \(W = 0.086 \times L^{3.02}\)
b) Predicted weights:
At L = 30 cm: \[W = 0.086 \times 30^{3.02} = 0.086 \times 24,411 = 2,099 \text{ g} = 2.1 \text{ kg}\]
At L = 50 cm: \[W = 0.086 \times 50^{3.02} = 0.086 \times 125,893 = 10,827 \text{ g} = 10.8 \text{ kg}\]
c) Condition factor K:
Standard form: \(K = 100,000 \times \frac{W}{L^3}\) (or \(K = 10 \times \frac{W}{L^3}\) in relative form)
For L = 30 cm, W = 2.1 kg: \[K = \frac{1.0 \times 2100}{30^3} = \frac{2100}{27,000} = 0.078\]
For L = 50 cm, W = 10.8 kg: \[K = \frac{1.0 \times 10,800}{50^3} = \frac{10,800}{125,000} = 0.086\]
d) Growth pattern assessment:

b = 3.02 ≈ 3 → ISOMETRIC GROWTH
Fish maintains constant shape and density across size range
Weight increases proportionally to volume (L³)
Growth is homogeneous (no allometric deviation)
R² = 0.94 indicates excellent fit (94% of variation explained)

Biological interpretation: Red snapper shows uniform growth pattern; body proportions remain consistent from juvenile to adult

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Question 4.4 (Statistical Analysis)
You collected LWR data on 100 sardines. Propose: a) Statistical methods to fit LWR b) How to test for isometry (b = 3) c) Uncertainty quantification approach

Model Answer:
a) Statistical fitting methods:
Method 1: Log-linear regression (Most Common) - Transform: \(\ln(W) = \ln(a) + b \times \ln(L)\) - Fit OLS regression on log-transformed data - Advantages: Linear model, easy interpretation - Disadvantages: Assumes log-normal error structure
Method 2: Power-law regression (Direct) - Fit \(W = aL^b\) directly using non-linear regression - Advantages: Models original scale; avoids log-transformation bias - Disadvantages: Requires iterative algorithms (R: nls(), nlme())
Method 3: Bayesian approach - Specify prior distributions for a and b - Update with likelihood from data - Advantages: Incorporate prior knowledge; full posterior uncertainty - Disadvantages: More computationally intensive
b) Test for isometry (H₀: b = 3):
Approach 1: Confidence interval - Fit regression, extract 95% CI for b coefficient - If CI contains 3 → isometric (fail to reject H₀) - If CI excludes 3 → allometric (reject H₀)
Approach 2: t-test \[t = \frac{b - 3}{SE_b}\] where \(SE_b\) = standard error of b coefficient

If |t| > critical value → significantly different from 3
Disadvantage: Low statistical power with this design

Approach 3: Constraint regression - Fit both models: (1) unconstrained; (2) constrained to b = 3 - Use likelihood ratio test to compare models - More powerful than simple t-test
c) Uncertainty quantification:
Method 1: Confidence intervals - Extract 95% CI for parameters a, b from regression output - Propagate to predicted weight: 95% CI on weight at each length
Method 2: Prediction intervals - Wider than confidence intervals (include prediction error) - Represents range for individual fish predictions
Method 3: Bootstrap - Resample 100 sardines (with replacement) 1000 times - Fit LWR to each resample - Calculate percentile CI for a and b from bootstrap distribution
Method 4: Bayesian posterior samples - Generate posterior samples of (a, b) - Compute credible intervals (typically 95%) - More intuitive interpretation: P(b = 3 | data)
Recommended approach: Log-linear regression with bootstrap CI on parameters

title: AQ 232 - Examination Questions
text:
Question 5.2 (Research Design)
Design a research project to investigate the relationship between ocean productivity (Chl-a from MODIS satellite data) and fish catch in Zanzibar coastal waters. Include:

Hypothesis and specific objectives
Sampling design (spatial, temporal)
Data collection protocol
Statistical analysis approach


Model Answer:
a) Hypothesis and objectives:
General Hypothesis: Ocean productivity (chlorophyll-a concentration) is positively related to fish catch in Zanzibar coastal waters, with variable lag between productivity changes and catch response.
Specific Objectives: 1. Quantify spatial-temporal patterns of Chl-a in Zanzibar EEZ 2. Characterize monthly variation in fish catch across coastal zones 3. Determine correlation between Chl-a and catch (synchronous and lagged) 4. Identify seasonal drivers of productivity-catch relationship
b) Sampling design:
Spatial: - Divide Zanzibar coastal zone into 5 grid cells (5°S-7°S; 39°E-42°E) - 1 km² resolution for satellite data; aggregate to 10 km for analysis - Focus on shelf waters (0-200 m depth)
Temporal: - Time period: 2015-2025 (10 years complete data coverage) - Satellite data: Monthly MODIS Aqua Chl-a (4 km resolution) - Catch data: Monthly landing records from fish markets (3 major ports) - Frequency: Monthly aggregations for analysis; seasonal analysis secondary
c) Data collection protocol:
Satellite data (MODIS Aqua): - Download monthly L3 standard mapped images from NASA Earthdata - Extract Chl-a values (mg/m³) for 5 grid cells - Quality control: Remove cloud-covered pixels, interpolate if <20% missing - Calculate zonal means and standard deviation
Catch data: - Survey landing sites: Dar es Salaam (main port), Zanzibar City, Bagamoyo - Record: Date, fish species, weight landed, vessel type, fishing area - Aggregate by month and grid cell using GPS coordinates if available - Cross-check against Ministry fisheries records
Environmental covariates: - Sea surface temperature (SST) from MODIS - Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) - Wind speed (from NOAA reanalysis)
d) Statistical analysis:
Step 1: Descriptive analysis - Time series plots of Chl-a and catch (overall and by grid cell) - Seasonal decomposition (trend + seasonal + residual components) - Calculate mean, SD, CV for each month/grid cell
Step 2: Correlation analysis
Synchronous (same month): \[\text{Catch}_t \sim \text{Chl-a}_t\]
Lagged (productivity leads catch): \[\text{Catch}_t \sim \text{Chl-a}_{t-1}, \text{Chl-a}_{t-2}, \text{Chl-a}_{t-3}\]

Calculate Pearson/Spearman correlations
Test for significance (α = 0.05)
Identify optimal lag period

Step 3: Regression modeling
Model structure (Poisson GLM or linear regression): \[\ln(\text{Catch}_t) = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{Chl-a}_{t-\tau} + \beta_2 \text{SST}_t + \beta_3 \text{Season}_t + \varepsilon_t\]
where τ = optimal lag identified in correlation analysis
Predictors: - Chl-a at optimal lag - SST (thermal preference) - Seasonal dummy variables (Jan-March, etc.) - Interannual trends
Model diagnostics: - Check residual normality, homoscedasticity - Test for temporal autocorrelation (Durbin-Watson) - Assess multicollinearity (VIF < 5) - Cross-validation: Split data 80/20, assess prediction error
Step 4: Spatial analysis

text:
2. Acoustic Surveys

The hydroacoustic survey uses an echo sounder to conduct acoustic biomass estimation.
It is widely used for assessing pelagic fish stocks (e.g., sardines, anchovies, herring, mackerel, tuna).

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
2. Acoustic Surveys

In practice for fish stock assessment, acoustic surveys are used to estimate fish stock.
These surveys are used to estimate the abundance of fish species that form schools in the water column.
They are particularly useful for pelagic species that are difficult to sample with traditional trawl surveys.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Acoustic Surveys: Key Terms

Acoustic survey - A survey that uses acoustic sound to estimate fish stock.
Echo sounder - A device that uses sound waves to detect fish.
Echo - A sound wave that is reflected back to the sounder.
Hydroacoustic survey - A survey that uses hydroacoustic sound to estimate fish stock.
Hydroacoustic means using sound in water.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Acoustic survey methodology

An acoustic transducer emits a brief, focused pulse of sound into the water.
If the sound encounters objects that are of different density than the surrounding medium, such as fish, they reflect some sound back toward the source.
The time it takes for the echo to return is used to calculate the distance to the object.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Acoustic survey methodology…

These echoes provide information on fish size, location, and abundance.
The basic components of the scientific echo sounder hardware function is to transmit the sound, receive, filter and amplify, record, and analyze the echoes.
While there are many manufacturers of commercially available fish-finders, quantitative analysis requires that measurements be made with calibrated echo sounder equipment, having high signal-to-noise ratios.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Principle of echo sounding

Everything scattered in the water column reflects sound waves depending on the frequency of the waves.
The higher frequency the shorter the wave length.
Therefore frequencies > 200 KHz can produce echo from plankton.
For fishes, a lower frequency < 200 KHz is used

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Conditions for echo sounding

Suitable for small pelagic fish stocks (big pelagic fishes eg. Tuna swim very fast and therefore the method becomes unsuitable).
The behavior of the fish to be assessed must be known

e.g the distribution of the fish in the water column at different times
The reaction of the fish towards the fishing boat should also be taken into account.

The use of a smaller boat towed by the bigger vessel to carry the transducer helps to detect fish which are frightened by the vessel.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Limitations of echo sounders

Sound beam interference by sound scatters eg. temperature stratification, air bubbles, sediments, debris, vegetation
Unsuitable for very shallow depths because of the blind zone that exists a few meters below the transducer depending on the diameter of the transducer and the frequency of the sound waves.

The larger the diameter the larger the zone.
Very deep waters calls for a stronger pulse generating echo sounder

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
3. Underwater Visual Census Survey (UVCS)

The more traditional method in which diver count fish along transects
It involves an observer, equipped with SCUBA gear, estimating the abundance of fish within a given area (the belt transect).
A multitude of factors, including fish mobility and habitat complexity, have been shown to effect the precision of the counting technique.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Applications of UVCS


Best suited for:
- Reef fish communities
- Shallow coastal waters
- Clear water environments
- Surface schooling species (tuna, sardines)

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Underwater Methods


Belt Transect Method:

Diver swims along fixed transect (e.g., 50 m × 5 m)
Records all fish within belt width
Estimates size classes
Multiple transects per site


Point Count Method:

Diver remains stationary
Counts fish within cylinder (e.g., 7.5 m radius)
Records species, size, abundance
Less affected by fish flight behavior

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Advantages & disadvantages of UVCS


Advantages:

Direct observation
Species identification possible
Behavioral information
Relatively low cost
Good for complex habitats (reefs)


Disadvantages:

Limited to clear, shallow water
Weather and visibility dependent
Observer bias
Diver safety concerns
Small spatial coverage
Fish behavior affects counts

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
4. Catch per unit effort (CPUE)

CPUE is catch obtained per standardized unit of fishing effort
Used as an index of abundance (relative, not absolute)
Catch rate (CPUE) is frequently and single most useful index for long-term monitoring of a fishery

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
4. Catch per unit effort (CPUE)…
Formula:
\[\text{CPUE} = \frac{\text{Total Catch}}{\text{Total Effort}}\]
Effort units:

Fishing hours or days at sea
Number of hooks (longline)
Number of fishers
Number of vessels
Number of gears

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
4. Catch per unit effort (CPUE)…

Changes in CPUE may give an indication of what is happening to the fish stock size
In theory, a constant trend of CPUE values represents a stable stock
A rising trend indicates an increasing stock
Increases in CPUE may mean that a fish stock is recovering and more fishing effort can be applied.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
4. Catch per unit effort (CPUE)…

A falling trend signifies a declining stock
A declines in CPUE may mean that the fish population cannot support the level of harvesting.
However, a falling trend does not necessarily indicate overfishing;

A fish stock will always decline from its initial high level when fishing occurs until it reaches an equilibrium level, when productivity balances the catch being taken.

CPUE can therefore be used as an index of stock abundance

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Advantages & disadvantages of CPUE
Advantages:

Uses existing commercial data
Cost-effective
Long time series available in many areas
Large spatial coverage
Real-time updates possible

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Advantages & disadvantages of CPUE
Disadvantages:

Differences regarding interpretation of fishing effort
Changes in actual or effective effort as a result of technological development
Also influenced by skills, experience
Affected by fisher behavior
May not reflect true abundance
Reporting biases
It is also difficult to know what factors of the fishing operations are important to measure
It is difficult to keep up with fishery changes
eg. CPUE could be altered without it being reflected on the stock size

A boat may install a more powerful motor

Or change from day to night fishing.

Not useful for measuring changes in the stock size of schooling fish species

eg. a pelagic species which schools at the surface can be easily seen from fishing boats or spotter planes therefore can be caught in bulk by purse seine nets.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
5. Mark-Recapture Methods

Is a Relative Fish abundance estimation
It involves capturing, marking, release and recapturing
The basic concept is that;

The ratio of recaptures in the second sample is equivalent to the proportion of those that were marked during the first sampling occasion to the whole population.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
5. Mark-Recapture Methods…

Then, estimation of population size (N) will be;

\[
\frac{m_2}{n_2} = \frac{n_1}{N}
\]

Sample 1 – marked and released

\(n_1\) = number captured and marked on the 1st sampling occasion

Sample 2 - number of recaptures recorded

\(n_2\) = number captured on the second sampling occasion
\(m_2\) = number of recaptures on the second occasion

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Assumptions for mark recapture method

The population is closed so that N remains constant

i.e. there is no movement in or out by birth, death, immigration or recruitment

All the fish have the same probability of being caught
Marked and unmarked fish have equal capture probability
The second sample is a random sample of the population
No marks of fish are lost between the sampling occasions
No marks go unrecorded during the second sampling
Marks do not affect survival

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Advantages & disadvantages of Mark-Recapture


Advantages:

Direct abundance estimate
Provides movement information
Estimates survival rates
Useful for discrete populations


Disadvantages:

Tagging stress and mortality
Tag loss or shedding
Expensive and labor-intensive
Assumption violations is common
Limited to feasible population sizes

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Mark-Recapture: Example 1
Problem:
500 tilapia are captured, marked, and released in Lake Victoria. One week later, 200 fish are recaptured, of these, 25 have marks. Find the population estimate in the lake.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Solution
Using the mark-recapture formula:
\[\frac{m_2}{n_2} = \frac{n_1}{N}\]
Where:

\(n_1 = 500\) (marked fish released)
\(n_2 = 200\) (fish recaptured)
\(m_2 = 25\) (marked fish recaptured)
\(N\) = ??? (unknown population size)

Rearranging the formula to solve for \(N\): \[N = \frac{n_1 \times n_2}{m_2}\] Substituting the values: \[N = \frac{500 \times 200}{25} = 4000\]
The estimated population size of tilapia in Lake Victoria is 4000 fishes.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Mark-Recapture: Example 2
In a capture-recapture process, 200 fishes were tagged. From the capture results, the game warden estimates that, the lake contains 2500 fishes. What percentage of fishes were tagged?

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Solution
Let p be the percent of tagged fishes;
\[
\frac{n_1}{N} = \frac{p}{100}
\]
\(\frac{200}{2500}=\frac{p}{100}\)
\(p = 8\%\)

About \(8\%\) of fishes were tagged

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
6. Depletion Methods

This method is mainly used for shell fish fishery i.e Octopus
The method uses either of the two models i.e Leslie and DeLury methods which depend upon the following assumptions;
Fishing (or sampling) must take a significant proportion of the population causing a depletion

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
6. Depletion method…

The decrease in catch per unit effort is proportional to;

The reduction in the population

Catchability of fish remains constant

Units of effort (or fishing gear) do not compete with one another - remains the same

The entire population is available to the fishery

There is no recruitment, natural mortality, immigration or emigration in the population.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
6. Depletion method…

It involves the removal of individuals from a stock and measuring the resulting decrease in relative abundance using CPUE as an abundance index.
It involves fishing on a closed population in which there is no immigration and emigration
Time interval is short enough to ignore losses due to natural mortality.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
6. Depletion method…
Leslie Method:
\[
\frac{C_t}{f_t} = q(N_o - IC)
\tag{1}\]
Where;

\(C_t\) = number of fish caught at time t
\(f_t\) = effort expended in taking \(C_t\)
\(\frac{C_t}{f_t}\) = catch per unit effort at time t (CPUE)
\(N_o\) = initial population size
\(q\) = catchability
\(IC\) = accumulated catch

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
6. Depletion method…
Or the Leslie formula can be expressed as;
\[
C_t = qN_0 - q\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}C_i
\tag{2}\]
Where:

\(C_t\) = Catch in period \(t\)
\(q\) = Catchability coefficient
\(N_0\) = Initial population size
\(\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}C_i\) = Cumulative catch up to time \(t-1\)
Then, plot \(C_t\) vs. cumulative catch; y-intercept = \(qN_0\), slope = \(-q\)

text:
7. Pelagic Egg and Larval Surveys
Principle:

Sample ichthyoplankton (fish eggs and larvae)
Estimate spawning stock biomass from egg production

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
7. Pelagic Egg and Larval Surveys..
Daily Egg Production Method (DEPM):
\[SSB = \frac{P_0 \times A}{R \times S \times F}\]
Where:

\(SSB\) = Spawning stock biomass
\(P_0\) = Daily egg production per unit area
\(A\) = Spawning area
\(R\) = Sex ratio (proportion female)
\(S\) = Spawning fraction (proportion spawning per day)
\(F\) = Batch fecundity (eggs per spawning female)

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Parameter interpretation
\(P_0\) (Daily Egg Production): Measures spawning intensity in the survey area. Higher \(P_0\) indicates active spawning; reflects reproductive output per unit spawning habitat.
\(A\) (Spawning Area): Geographic extent of the spawning ground. Larger area = greater total egg production. Accurate delineation is critical.
\(R\) (Sex Ratio): Only females produce eggs. Must adjust for proportion of females in spawning population.
\(S\) (Spawning Fraction): Not all females spawn on a given day. Varies by species and environmental conditions. Lower \(S\) = smaller daily fraction of stock spawning.
\(F\) (Batch Fecundity): Individual female reproductive capacity. Higher \(F\) = fewer females needed to produce observed eggs. Critical parameter often determined from histological analysis.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Sample question 1:
A sardine spawning survey in Tanzanian coastal waters collected the following data:

Daily egg production per unit area (\(P_0\)) = 450 eggs/m²/day
Spawning area (\(A\)) = 5,000 km²
Sex ratio (\(R\)) = 0.52 (52% female)
Spawning fraction (\(S\)) = 0.35 (35% spawn per day)
Batch fecundity (\(F\)) = 12,000 eggs/female

Calculate the spawning stock biomass (SSB) of sardine given that each sardine egg weighs ~0.75 mg.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Answer:
First, convert spawning area to m²: \[A = 5,000 \text{ km}^2 = 5,000 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^2 = 5 \times 10^9 \text{ m}^2\]
Apply DEPM formula: \[SSB = \frac{450 \times 5 \times 10^9}{0.52 \times 0.35 \times 12,000}\]
\[SSB = \frac{2.25 \times 10^{12}}{2,184} = 1.03 \times 10^9 \text{ eggs}\]
Converting to biomass (sardine eggs ~0.75 mg = 0.00075 g per egg): \[1.03 \times 10^9 \text{ eggs} \times 0.00075 \text{ g/egg} = 7.73 \times 10^8 \text{ g}\]
Convert to tonnes (1 tonne = \(10^6\) g): \[\frac{7.73 \times 10^8 \text{ g}}{10^6 \text{ g/tonne}} = 773 \text{ tonnes}\]
\[SSB \approx 773 \text{ tonnes}\]

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Introduction

Fish stock assessment was developed in the temperate regions where there are very few species of fish.
It was based on a single species
However, such a consideration is not very applicable for tropical fisheries where we have multi-species fisheries because;

Different species are mixed up
There is very high interaction among species

In such situation, fish populations are divided into stocks (unit stock) for management and assessment purposes
Understanding the distribution, abundance, and methods for estimating stock parameters is important for effective stock assessment and sustainable fisheries management.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Unit Stock

A unit stock is a population of fish, either of a single or different species, grouped together for assessment purposes which may or may not include all the fish in a stock.
A unit stock is a group of fish that:

Share a common gene pool – can interbreed
Occupy a defined geographical area – have a specific distribution
Exhibit similar life history traits – growth, reproduction, mortality
Are subject to similar fishing pressures – exploited by the same fisheries
Are managed as a single entity – for conservation and exploitation, – Can be managed independently from other stocks

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Determination of a Unit Stock

Unit stocks can be determined through various biological and ecological characteristics, including:

Distribution patterns – Where unit stocks are located
Spawning behavior – Different stocks spawn in different areas
Population parameters – Recruitment, growth and mortality rates, morphometric differences
Physiological traits – Temperature at hatching, vertebrae structure, scale decorations, parasite types

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Distribution and Abundance
Geographic Distribution

Geographic distribution refers to the spatial area where a fish stock is found, including the boundaries of its range.

Key concepts:

Fish populations are not uniformly distributed across all suitable habitats
Distribution patterns change seasonally (spawning, feeding, wintering areas)
Some species have discrete distributions while others have overlapping ranges
Distribution limits are determined by temperature, salinity, bathymetry, and food availability

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Geographic Distribution
Examples:

Migratory species (salmon) move between coastal and riverine habitats
Demersal species (bottom-dwelling) have specific depth distributions
Pelagic species distribute widely in open water

Management implications:

Fishing effort should target areas of highest concentration
Seasonal closures may protect aggregations during vulnerable periods
International boundaries may complicate management of stocks crossing borders

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
section: Spatial and Temporal Variation in Abundance
text:
Spatial and Temporal Variation in Abundance
Temporal Variation:

Seasonal changes - Abundance fluctuates with feeding, spawning, and migration cycles
Interannual variation - Year-to-year changes in recruitment and survival
Long-term trends - Decadal-scale changes related to fishing pressure or environmental conditions

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Spatial and Temporal Variation…
Spatial Variation:

Patchiness - Fish concentrate in certain areas (spawning grounds, feeding areas)
Gradients - Density changes across depth, latitude, or habitat types
Hotspots - Areas of consistently high abundance

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Spatial and Temporal Variation…
Measurement challenges:

Detecting aggregations requires spatially intensive sampling
Small-scale variability requires high sampling effort to quantify accurately
Temporal dynamics require time series of observations

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
section: Habitat Requirements and Factors Affecting Distribution
text:
Habitat Requirements and Factors Affecting Distribution
Abiotic Factors:

Temperature - Most critical factor; thermal preferences vary by species
Salinity - Freshwater, brackish, or marine preferences
Dissolved oxygen - Required for respiration; anaerobic zones are avoided
Bathymetry - Depth preferences related to light and pressure tolerance
Substrate type - Bottom type affects benthic food availability

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Habitat Requirements…
Biotic Factors:

Food availability - Distribution follows food resources
Predation risk - Avoidance of predator-rich areas
Competition - Space partitioning with other species
Reproductive habitat - Essential for spawning and nursery grounds

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Habitat Requirements…
Habitat Quality:

Optimal habitat supports higher population densities
Marginal habitat may be temporarily occupied but has lower reproductive success
Loss or degradation of critical habitat can limit population size

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Environmental Influences on Stock Distribution
Physical Oceanography:

Ocean currents transport larvae and affect distribution
Upwelling events create productive feeding areas
Coastal current patterns structure population distributions

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Environmental Influences…
Climate and Weather:

Climate change shifts suitable habitat ranges
Seasonal weather events (storms, cold snaps) cause temporary distribution changes
Long-term climate trends alter distribution boundaries

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
section: Straddling stock and highly migratory fish stock
text:
Straddling stock and highly migratory fish stock

With 1982’s United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), coastal nations were given the right to manage fisheries within their Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ)
But of course, fish don’t adhere to imaginary lines in the ocean.
The management of two groups – straddling and highly migratory fish stocks became problem after the 1982 Convention.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Straddling stock

Straddling stocks are fish stocks that migrate across more than one Exclusive Economic Exclusion Zone (EEZ) and the high seas

Straddling stocks is the stocks of fish which migrate between, or occur in both, the EEZ of one or more states and the high seas

Fish stocks that migrate through, or occur in more than one exclusive economic zone.
They include species such as swordfish and marlin.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Highly migratory fishes

Highly migratory fishes are the ones that travel long distances across international waters
These include tuna and tuna-like species such as yellowfin tuna, bigeye tuna, and skipjack.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
section: Management of Straddling stock and Highly migratory fishes
text:
Management of Straddling stock and Highly migratory fishes

Management of the straddling stock and highly migratory fishes is a shared responsibility between coastal states and the international community.
The 1995 United Nations Fish Stocks Agreement (UNFSA), an international treaty designed to further implement provisions of the 1982 Convention which;

Ensure the long-term conservation and sustainable use of straddling fish stocks and highly migratory fish stocks

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Management…

Sovereign responsibility must be worked out in collaboration with neighboring coastal states and fishing entities.
Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMOs) are established to manage these stocks collaboratively.
Transboundary stock range in the EEZs of at least two countries.
A stock can be both transboundary and straddling.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Mixed stock

A mixed stock occurs when individuals from two or more genetically distinct populations are found together in the same geographic area
Fish from multiple spawning populations intermingle during feeding, migration, or overwintering
Cannot be easily distinguished visually but are genetically or demographically separate

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Common Scenarios for Mixed Stock
1. Feeding Aggregations

Fish from different spawning stocks congregate in productive feeding grounds
Example: Salmon from multiple rivers feeding together in the ocean

2. Migratory Overlap

Different populations share migration routes
Example: Tuna stocks from different ocean regions mixing along migration corridors

3. Seasonal Mixing

Populations separate for spawning but mix at other times
Example: Herring from different spawning grounds overwintering together

text:

Genetic markers (microsatellites)

Morphometric analysis (body shape differences)
Tagging studies (track individual movements)

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Three Core Data Requirements
A successful stock assessment needs three types of data:








Data type
Question it answers
Typical examples




Catch data
How much is being removed?
Landings, discards, bycatch


Relative abundance data
Is the stock increasing or decreasing?
CPUE, survey indices


Life history data
How does the species grow, mature and die?
Age, growth, maturity, mortality



Both fishery-dependent and fishery-independent sources contribute to meeting these requirements.

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Fishery-Dependent vs. Fishery-Independent









Fishery-dependent
Fishery-independent




Source
The fishing process itself
Scientific research activities


Who collects
Fishers, port agents, observers
Scientists with standardized gear


Coverage
Continuous, all fishing grounds
Periodic, fixed stations


Cost
Low (uses existing operations)
High (vessels, equipment, staff)


Main risk
Biased by fisher behaviour
Short time series, limited area



Why both are important: one is continuous and cheap; the other is unbiased and standardized. Together they give robust abundance estimates.

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
What Is Fishery-Dependent Data?
Data collected directly from the fishing process. Fishers and fishing operations are the data source.
Common sources:

Landing records — catch weights recorded at ports and markets
Portside sampling — biological samples taken at landing sites
Onboard observers — scientists or government staff on fishing vessels
Logbooks and trip reports — fisher-kept records of catch and effort
Vessel monitoring systems (VMS) — electronic tracking of vessel position
Telephone surveys — recall interviews with fishers

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Landing Records & Portside Sampling


Landing Records

Result directly from the sale of fish at ports
Provide landed catch only
Usually recorded as total weight, not numbers
Species identified and weighed daily


Portside Sampling

Done by port agents / portside observers
Fish measured for size at the dock
Age from growth rings in scales or otoliths (like tree rings)
Called a creel survey in recreational fisheries
Sample is raised to the total catch by species and gear

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Onboard Observers


Purpose

Government personnel accompany commercial vessels
Monitor how fishers interact with target and non-target species
Record fishing location, gear configuration and depth


Data Collected

Size and age of sampled catch
Bycatch — incidental catch of non-target species
Discards — fish returned to the sea
Biological samples: maturity, stomach contents

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Logbooks, VMS & Telephone Surveys


Logbooks & Trip Reports

Mandatory or voluntary records kept by fishers
Less reliable than landings and observer data for catch weight and numbers
Valuable for spatial distribution and fishing effort across seasons
VMS automatically records vessel location and movement


Telephone Surveys

Primary method for recreational fisheries
Widely used in small-scale fisheries to record catch numbers, location and size
Useful when on-site sampling is impractical

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
From Logbooks to CPUE
Catch Per Unit Effort (CPUE) converts catch and effort records into an abundance index:
CPUE=CatchEffort\text{CPUE} = \frac{\text{Catch}}{\text{Effort}}

Standardize for vessel type, fishing method and season
Trend over time as a proxy for changes in abundance
Effort may be fishing days, hours trawled, number of hooks, or number of fishers

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Fishery-Dependent Data: Strengths & Weaknesses


✅ Advantages

Continuous coverage — every fishing day
Cost-effective — uses existing operations
Large spatial scale — all fishing grounds
Timely — available quickly for decisions
Long time series — often 10+ years


⚠️ Disadvantages

Biased — fishers target abundance, not random sampling
Under- or mis-reporting of catches
Informal sector often unrecorded
Technology creep — vessels become more efficient
Misses small, juvenile or rare fish

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
What Is Fishery-Independent Data?
Data collected from research activities that do not involve commercial harvesting. Scientists design and run the surveys.
Common sources:

Research trawl and seine surveys — standardized gear on a fixed grid
Acoustic surveys — echo sounders detect and quantify schooling fish
Visual surveys — divers or submersibles observe fish
Larval / egg surveys — estimate spawning stock from pelagic eggs and larvae
Mark–recapture (tagging) studies — estimate movement, growth and mortality
Remote sensing — satellite data on chlorophyll, temperature and habitat

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Research Survey Approaches


Design

Standardized gear: trawls, seines, hydroacoustics, video
Samples collected throughout the range of the target fish
Can target multiple species or a single species
Can target life stages (e.g. juvenile year classes)


Outputs

Abundance indices for stock assessment
Size, age and maturity information from the stock
Fish counted, measured and aged on every station
Absolute or relative abundance estimates

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Survey Examples in Practice








Survey
How it works
What it produces




Trawl survey
Annual cruise, standardized trawl, fixed station grid
Absolute or relative abundance index, length and age data


Acoustic survey
Calibrated echo sounder along transects (e.g. sardines)
Backscatter converted to stock biomass


Visual census
Divers swim fixed reef transects, repeated yearly
Fish density and size distribution

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Mark and Recapture Studies
A specialized research method for estimating population parameters. It provides estimates of:

Movement and migration patterns
Growth rates
Natural mortality
Discard mortality
Population size (from the proportion of marked fish recaptured)

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Fishery-Independent Data: Strengths & Weaknesses


✅ Advantages

Unbiased — designed to represent the whole population
Standardized protocols across years
Covers unfished areas
All life stages — juveniles, adults, spawners
Independent of fisher behaviour


⚠️ Disadvantages

High cost — vessel, equipment, trained staff
Intermittent — seasonal or annual, not continuous
Limited spatial coverage
Slow turnaround — often 6–12 months
Short time series — often only 5–10 years

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Why Do We Need Them?
In small-scale fisheries, catch is landed at many scattered sites and is hard to count completely.
Two linked surveys solve this problem:

Frame survey — a census of fishing capacity (boats, gear, fishers, sites)
Catch Assessment Survey (CAS) — a sample of actual catches


The frame survey tells us how big the fishery is; the CAS tells us how much each unit catches. Combined, they give the total catch.

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Fisheries Frame Survey


Definition

A census of all fishing vessels and gear types
Covers all homeports and fishing sites in the assessment area
Provides a static snapshot of the fishery


Supplementary Information

Fishing trip patterns and frequency
Seasonal gear use
Socio-economic information about fishing communities
Demographic profile of fishers

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Frame Survey: What Is Collected


Landing Sites & Fleet

Number of operational landing sites
Number of active fishers
Number and type of fishing crafts
Propulsion (motorized, manual)

Facilities & Services

Infrastructure at landing sites
Services from fisheries staff and Beach Management Units (BMUs)


Gear

Types and sizes of fishing gears
Operation modes for each gear type

Management Use

Recommendations for fishery development and management
Raising factors for scaling up CAS data to total catch

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Frame Survey: Planning & Quality Assurance


Survey Design

Define boat and gear categories
Decide sequential vs. concurrent gear use
Decide whether new gear types are included


Field Operations

Plan visits to all landing ports
Develop protocols for interviewing fishers and village leaders
Ensure complete vessel and gear counts


Quality Control

Train collectors with clear, unambiguous instructions
Explain each recording form’s purpose
Cross-check data and resolve serious discrepancies

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Limitations of Frame Surveys


Static Snapshot

Valid only at the time of the survey
Represents a single point in time


Impact of Change

Changes in the number of boats
New gear types introduced
Shifts in fishing effort or patterns




Rapid change makes raising factors unreliable for estimating total effort, so frame surveys must be repeated regularly.

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Catch Assessment Surveys (CAS)


What Is a CAS?

Survey designed to estimate total catch
Based on sampling a portion of landing sites or fishing effort
Records catch from selected sites or vessels


Why It Matters

Bridges the gap between an infeasible census and incomplete data
Gives catch estimates with quantified uncertainty
Supports accurate monitoring of harvest levels
Essential for ecosystem-based management

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
CAS Data Collection
Information recorded for each sample:

Total catch weight by species and gear type
Length and age composition of the catch
Sex and maturity information
Bycatch and discards estimates
Date, location and gear type

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
CAS vs. Frame Survey









Frame survey
Catch assessment survey




Approach
Census (all boats and gear)
Sample (selected sites / vessels)


Tells us
Fishing capacity and infrastructure
Actual catch and biology


Role
Defines the population; supplies raising factors
Supplies the sample to be raised


Frequency
Periodic (e.g. every few years)
Continuous / regular

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Raising Factor: Worked Example
Raising factor=Total boats (frame survey)Boats sampled (CAS)\text{Raising factor} = \frac{\text{Total boats (frame survey)}}{\text{Boats sampled (CAS)}}

Frame survey identifies 100 fishing boats at a landing site
CAS samples the catch of 20 boats
Raising factor =100÷20=5= 100 \div 20 = 5
Total catch == sample catch ×\times 5

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Integrating the Data


Key Data Components

Fisheries statistics — catch and effort
Frame survey data — fleet and gear
Biological data — from research surveys and port sampling

Definition of key terms

Fish Catch is the total number or weight of fish captured from an area over a period of time.
This includes fish that are caught but released or discarded instead of being landed.
Carrying Capacity is amount of fish that a specific habitat can support.
Bycatch is the harvest of fish or animals other than the species for which the fishing gear was intended

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Definition of key terms…

Catch Per Unit Effort (CPUE) is the quantity of fish caught (in number or in weight) with one standard unit of fishing effort.
Effort can be number of fishing gear or vessel, length of time used during fishing, number of fishermen etc.
e.g. number of fish taken per 1000 hooks per day or weight of fish taken per hour of trawling.
CPUE is often considered as an index of fish biomass (or abundance).
CPUE is also referred to as catch rate

text:
Definition of key terms…

Effort is the amount of time and fishing power used to harvest fish.
Fishing power includes gear size, boat size, and horsepower.

Spawning rate is the number of eggs and sperm released per unit time

Recruitment the number of new young fish that enter a population in a given year.
Morphometrics these are measurements which characterize the form, shape and appearance of a fish.
Difference in morphometrics, such as colouration, can be used to distinguish different stocks of the same species.

title: AF 603 – Fish population dynamics and stock assessment
text:
Definition of key terms…

Maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is theoretical harvest of a fish species that can be taken over an indefinite period.
MSY theoretically aims to maintain the population size at the point of maximum growth rate by harvesting the individuals that would normally be added to the population.
MSY has been widely criticized and has led to the collapse of many fisheries, as it ignores size, age, reproductive capacity, and fishing effort.

Fish mortality is a parameter that account for the loss of fish in a fish stock through death.
The mortality can be divided into two types;

Natural mortality – the removal of fish from stock due to causes not associated with fishing.

It is denoted by (F) in fisheries models.
Mortality rate or death rate is a measure of the number of deaths in a particular population per unit time.
Mortality rate is the rate at which fish die, typically shown as a percentage.

Nt+1=Nt+Rt−Mt−CtN_{t+1} = N_t + R_t - M_t - C_t
What each term means:

Nt+1N_{t+1} = Population next year
NtN_t = Current population

Next year’s population = This year’s fish + New recruits - Deaths from disease/predation - Fish caught by fishers

Lose 1,500 to natural causes
Remove 2,000 by fishing

Growth: – The increase in size and weight of individual fish as they age

Fastest when young (more energy to growth)
Slows with age (more energy to reproduction)
Asymptotic (approaches maximum)
Affected by environment and density

title: AF 603: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Growth (G)…
Von Bertalanffy Growth Model:
Lt=L∞(1−e−K(t−t0))L_t = L_\infty(1 - e^{-K(t-t_0)})
Where:

LtL_t = Length at age t (what we are trying to predict)
L∞L_\infty = Length at infinity – Asymptotic length (maximum length fish can theoretically reach)
KK = Growth rate coefficient (how fast fish approach maximum length)
t=Aget = Age
t0t_0 = Theoretical age at zero length (usually close to 0)

title: AF 603: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Logic Behind Von Bertalanffy Model
The Biology:

Fish grow fastest when young - At age 0, the term (1−e−K(t−t0))(1 - e^{-K(t-t_0)}) is close to 0, so length is small
Growth slows with age - As fish get older, they approach L∞L_\infty asymptotically (get closer to the maximum length but never quite reach it)
Approaches a maximum - No matter how old the fish gets, it cannot exceed L∞L_\infty
Growth rate controlled by K - A larger KK = fish reach maximum size faster; smaller KK = slower growth

title: AF 603: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Why Von Bertalanffy Model realistic?

Fish actually DO grow quickly early and slow down with age
Energy allocation shifts from growth to reproduction
Food becomes limiting relative to body size

The Exponential Growth Model describes population growth when there are no resource limitations.

\(t\) = time


What it means:

If \(r > 0\): population grows exponentially
If \(r = 0\): population stable
If \(r < 0\): population declines or shrink

What is Stock-Recruitment?

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Beverton-Holt Model

The Beverton-Holt model is a commonly used stock-recruitment relationship in fisheries science.

Formula:
\[R_t = \frac{aS_t}{1 + bS_t}\]
Where:

\(R_t\) = recruitment at time t
\(S_t\) = spawning stock size
\(a\) = productivity parameter (maximum recruitment potential)
\(b\) = density-dependent parameter (strength of density dependence)

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Beverton-Holt Model…


Characteristics:

Recruitment increases with spawners
Recruitment plateaus at high spawning stock (asymptotic)
Maximum recruitment = \(a/b\)
Good for species with strong density-dependent effects

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
How Beverton-Holt Works


At low spawning stock (S_t small):

Recruitment increases nearly linearly with spawners
Few density-dependent effects
Each new spawner adds substantially to recruitment


At high spawning stock (S_t large):

Recruitment plateaus (approaches maximum)
Density-dependent effects dominate
Competition for food/space reduces per-capita recruitment
Additional spawners add little to total recruitment

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Mathematical insight of Beverton-Holt model


Formula:
\[R_t = \frac{aS_t}{1 + bS_t}\]


When \(S_t = 0\): \(R_t = 0\) (no spawners = no recruitment)
When \(S_t\) → ∞: \(R_t\) → \(a/b\) (maximum recruitment)

How Population Density Matters

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
What is Density Dependence?
Density Dependence:– When vital rates (growth, survival, reproduction) depend on population density
How it works:

High density → increased competition
Competition for food, space, mates
Reduced growth and survival
Lower recruitment

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Density Dependence…
Equation:
\[\text{Vital Rate} = f(\text{Population Size})\]
Meaning: Vital Rate is a function of Population Size

The vital rate changes depends on how many fish are in the population
It is a mathematical function where population size is the input

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Density Dependence…
Example 1: Growth Rate
\[Growth~Rate = f(Population~Size)\]

Small population: Fish have plenty of food → Fast growth
Large population: Competition for food → Slow growth
Same species, different growth rate based on population density

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Density Dependence…
Example 2: Survival Rate
\[Survival~Rate = f(Population~Size)\]

Small population: Low mortality (abundant resources) → High survival
Large population: High mortality (starvation, disease) → Low survival

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Density Dependence…
Example 3: Reproduction Rate
\[Reproduction~Rate = f(Population~Size)\]

Small population: Fish produce many eggs → High recruitment
Large population: Fish produce fewer eggs → Low recruitment

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Density Dependence…
In contrast, WITHOUT density dependence:
\[Vital~Rate = constant\]

Vital Rate does not change with population size

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Summary of Density Dependence
Growth:

Dense populations grow slower
Limited food per fish
Smaller fish at same age

Survival:

Dense populations have higher mortality
Starvation increases
Disease spreads easier

Reproduction:

Dense populations produce fewer recruits
Smaller eggs
Lower reproductive success
