title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Introduction

Estimating fish stock abundance is important for sustainable fisheries management.
Various methods exist, each with strengths and limitations.
Choice of method depends on species, habitat, data availability, and resources.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Fish abundance

Fish abundance refers to the number of individuals in a fish population within a defined area.
It is a key metric for assessing the health and sustainability of fish stocks.
Accurate abundance estimates inform management decisions, such as setting catch limits and conservation measures.
Abundance can be expressed as:

Absolute abundance – Measure the actual number of fish in an area i.e Pond
Relative abundance – Estimate the number of fish at a given locality

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Fish abundance…

Abundance is not a fixed quantity – Varies from time to time (seasonal) due to;

Internal forces i.e births and deaths and
External forces i.e seasonal availability of food, changes in environmental conditions that may affect the population

It varies from place to place because of the heterogeneity of the environment

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Fish abundance…

Within the area of distribution the abundance of a population always vary – either grow (increase) or decline
The population may vary with season due to;

Births
Deaths

Seasonal migration (spawning, feeding and over-wintering) recruitment

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Fish migration

Fish migration is mass relocation by fish from one area or body of water to another.
Fish migrate;

On a regular basis

On time scales – from daily, seasonal, annually or

Longer, and over distances – from a few metres to thousands of kilometres.

Such migrations are usually done for feeding or to reproduce, but in other cases the reasons are unclear.
Migration affects local abundance estimates and must be considered in survey design.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Terminologies in fish migration

Diadromous – Fishes that migrate between the sea and freshwater.
Anadromous – Diadromous fishes which spend most of their lives in the sea and migrate to freshwater to breed (salmon, sea trout, shad, sea lampreys, sturgeons)
Catadromous – Diadromous fishes which spend most of their lives in freshwater and migrate to the sea to breed (eel, Salangidae, Galaxidae, Retropinnidae).
Amphidromous – Diadromous fishes which migrate from the sea to freshwater or vice versa, but not for the purpose of breeding (some Exocidae,Perca fluviatilis, some Mugilidae).

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Terminologies in fish migration…

Potamodromous – Migratory fishes that live and migrate wholly within freshwater systems (rivers, lakes, streams). They never enter marine environments e.g (trout, bream, Coregonoids)

Complete their entire life cycle in freshwater.
Migrate between different freshwater habitats for spawning, feeding, or overwintering

Their migration patterns are triggered by Water temperature changes, Flooding (access to floodplain habitats), Photoperiod (day length), Food availability, Spawning readiness

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Terminologies in fish migration…

Oceanodromous – Migratory fishes that live and migrate wholly within the sea (marine environment). They never enter freshwater. (cod, herring, capelin, tuna, mackerel).
Complete their entire life cycle in marine waters
Migrate between different ocean habitats for spawning, feeding, or seasonal movements
Migration distances can range from coastal movements to trans-oceanic journeys (thousands of kilometers)
Their migration patterns are triggered by Sea surface temperature gradients, Ocean current patterns (monsoons in Indian Ocean), Prey availability (following zooplankton blooms), Spawning readiness and lunar cycles, Upwelling events

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Methods for estimating fish abundance
1. Direct Methods (Surveys)

Trawl surveys, acoustic surveys, visual surveys
Provide absolute or relative abundance estimates
Require dedicated research vessels and equipment

2. Indirect Methods (Fishery-Dependent)

CPUE, mark-recapture, depletion methods
Use commercial fishery data
Cost-effective but subject to biases

3. Statistical Models

Virtual Population Analysis, integrated models
Combine multiple data sources
Require specialized software and expertise

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
1. Trawl Surveys–Swept area method

It is assumed that the area swept by the trawl is representative for the entire area over which the fishes are distributed.
That fish caught within the area swept by the trawl net is proportion to their abundance

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Trawl net



Trawl net is a conical bag with a wide mouth fitted with otter boards for horizontal opening and floats and weights for vertical opening.
This net sweeps the sea bed over a wide area.
The tail end of the gear where the fishes are collected is called codend.





Trawl Net

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Types of Trawl Nets

Trawl nets that are dragged on the sea floor are called bottom trawls.
Bottom trawl - Demersal species (snappers, groupers, flatfish)
Mid-water trawl - Pelagic species (sardines, herring)

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Swept area method
Principle of swept area method:

The mean catch (either in weight or in numbers) per unit of effort or per unit of area is an index of the stock abundance.
This index is converted into an absolute measure of biomass.

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Swept area method…
\[\frac{a}{A} = \frac{c}{B}\]

The biomass (B) is converted to absolute biomass by multiplying with constant R

\[\frac{a}{A}=\frac{c}{BR}\]

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Swept area method…
\[B = \frac{cA}{aR}\]
Where;
B = Biomass
a = area swept by the net
c = catch
A = area of distribution of the fish stock
R = retention rate of the net (0.5 - 0.8)

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Swept area method…

A trawl net is used to estimate the mean catch at a number of stations in a fish stock
A towed trawl net samples fish in an area (a) prescribed by the net’s effective width and distance traveled by the net

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Calculations on swept area method

Let
a be the area prescribed by the net h is the length of the net head rope
If the effective width of the net (w) is proportion to the head rope (e.g 0.6);
Then,
\(w = 0.6h\)

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Swept area method…

If the towing speed (v) and time for trawling (t) is known then, it is possible to calculate the distance (d) covered during towing

\[d = v\times t\]

Then, the area prescribed by the net during towing is \[a = w \times d\] \[a = w\times v\times t\]

After 0.5 hour of trawling at a speed of 2 km per hour, 3 tons of fish were caught by a trawl net with a head rope measuring 20m. If the retention rate of the net was 50% and only 0.6 of the head rope was making an effective width of the path, calculate the biomass of a fish stock of Solea solea distributed over an area of 4 km2

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
What is Length-Weight Relationship?

The mathematical relationship between fish body length and body weight
Different species have different relationships

Key idea:

Longer fish are generally heavier
But the relationship is NOT linear
Weight increases with the cube of length (cubic relationship) – Cube Law \[W \propto L^3\]

\[W = aL^3\]

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Weakness of Cube Law

Not all fish grow isometrically (b=3)
Some species get heavier (b>3) or lighter (b<3) as they grow
Body shape and condition affect weight gain
Environmental factors (food, habitat) also influence growth patterns

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Allometry

Allometry describes how body proportions change with size
In fish, allometric growth means weight does not increase exactly with cube of length
The general formula is: \[W = aL^b\]

Where:

\(W\) = weight
\(L\) = length
\(a\) = intercept
\(b\) = slope

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Logarithmic Form for allometric equation
Logarithmic form(linear regression):

\[W = aL^b\]
Taking log of both sides gives:

\[\log(W) = \log(a) + b \cdot \log(L)\]

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
What does ‘a’ mean?

Scale factor or intercept
Species-specific (different species have different values)
Related to fish condition and body shape
Heavier fish species have larger ‘a’ values

Example:

Nile Perch: \(a ≈ 0.0098\) (robust body)
Cichlid: \(a ≈ 0.005\) (slender body)
Same length, different weight due to different ‘a’

title: AQ 232: Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
What does ‘b’ mean?

Exponent or slope
Determines how weight scales with length
Typical range: 2.5 to 3.5

Interpretation:







b value
Meaning




b = 3
Isometric growth - Perfect cubic relationship


b > 3
Allometric growth (positive) - Fish gets proportionally heavier as it grows


b < 3
Allometric growth (negative) - Fish gets proportionally lighter as it grows

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
section: Fish Population Structure in Stock Assessment
text:
Fish Population Structure in Stock Assessment
Definition:
Population structure refers to the composition of the stock in terms of age, size, sex, and spatial distribution.
Key Components:

Age structure — proportion of fish in each age class (recruits, juveniles, adults, old fish)
Size distribution — length or weight frequency of individuals
Sex ratio — proportion of males vs. females
Spatial structure — distribution across fishing grounds and habitats
Spawning groups — location and timing of reproductive aggregations

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Why Population Structure Matters
Recruitment Assessment

Young age classes indicate strong recent recruitment
Absence of recruits signals poor spawning success
Tracks recovery or decline in population regeneration

Fishing Impact Detection

Depleted age structure (few old fish) indicates overfishing
Skewed toward juveniles may indicate selective harvest of adults
Size-selective fishing distorts natural length distribution

Productivity Prediction

Abundant reproductive-age fish = high reproductive output potential
Few spawners = reduced recruitment capacity and stock fragility
Age/size diversity = resilience to environmental variation

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Population Structure and Abundance Estimates
Total Abundance vs. Exploitable Abundance

Total abundance = count of all fish (recruits + juveniles + adults)
Exploitable stock = fish large enough to be caught legally
Population structure determines what fraction is harvestable

Example:

Total stock: 1 million fish
Age structure: 40% recruits (age 0), 35% juveniles (age 1–2), 25% adults (age 3+)
If only fish age 3+ are legally harvestable → Exploitable stock = 250,000 fish

Management implication: Total abundance alone is insufficient; must know age structure to estimate harvestable surplus

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Population Structure Drives Reference Points
Stock Status Indicators

Recruitment — abundance of young fish; indicates future stock potential
Spawning stock biomass (SSB) — total weight of reproductive fish; drivers of recruitment
Fishing mortality by age — which age classes are being removed most heavily

Biological Reference Points

Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) — age/size structure at equilibrium where catch is maximized
Limit reference points — minimum acceptable population structure to avoid collapse
Target reference points — desired age structure for long-term productivity

Without age/size data, these reference points cannot be calculated or monitored

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Population Structure Methods and Data
How to Measure Population Structure

Port sampling — collect length measurements and age-read scales/otoliths from landed fish
Research surveys — trawl or acoustic surveys collect size/age data from catches
Scale analysis — count growth rings (annuli) to determine age
Otolith analysis — read ear bones (more accurate for older fish)
Length-frequency distribution — estimate age from length using growth models

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Population Structure Indicators
Healthy Population Structure

Multiple age classes present (age 1–10+ depending on species)
Recruitment pulses visible (strong cohorts traceable as they age)
Abundant reproductive-age fish (age at maturity to older ages)
Size distribution follows growth model predictions

Warning Signs of Population Stress

Few or no recruits — poor reproduction or high juvenile mortality
Missing middle age classes — past years of poor recruitment or selective fishing
Very old fish rare — fishing removes before natural lifespan completed
Stunted size distribution — indicates overcrowding or poor nutrition

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Age Structure and Selective Fishing
Size-Selective Fishing Distorts Age Structure

Selective harvest of large fish → Population skews young; reproductive potential declines
Selective harvest of small fish → Reduces recruitment survival; fewer juveniles mature
Non-selective fishing → More balanced removal across age classes

Example (Snappers):

Unmanaged: Fishers harvest large, old fish preferentially (higher value)
Result: Population age structure becomes dominated by young, immature fish
Consequence: Recruitment crashes; stock cannot replace itself

Management response: Size/age restrictions (e.g., minimum/maximum landing size) restore age structure

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Population Structure and Ecosystem Effects
Food Web Implications

Juvenile fish: primary consumers, high mortality, feed on zooplankton
Intermediate fish: piscivorous, control juvenile populations
Large adult fish: apex predators, energy transfer efficiency

Loss of older fish:

Eliminates large predators → mesopredators increase → energy flow disrupted
Shifts diet composition (fewer large fish predate on smaller competitors)
Trophic cascades alter ecosystem structure

Rebuilding requires restoring age/size structure, not just total abundance

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
text:
Population Structure for Data-Limited Fisheries
When Resources are Limited:

Even simple length sampling at landing sites provides population structure
Length-frequency analysis can estimate trends in recruitment and fishing pressure
No age-reading required; length alone often sufficient for preliminary assessment

Example Application:

Monthly length samples from 100 fish at one landing site
Plot length-frequency distribution
Compare to previous years to track recruitment strength and fishing selectivity

title: AQ 232 – Fish Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment
section: Key Takeaway: Abundance + Structure = Complete Assessment
text:
Key Takeaway: Abundance + Structure = Complete Assessment
Why Population Structure is Essential:

Total abundance tells you how many fish; structure tells you if they can reproduce
Trends in recruitment indicate future stock health; can’t see without age data
Fishing selectivity invisible in total abundance; obvious in age structure
Reference points and harvest rules depend on knowing stock structure
Ecosystem impacts depend on preserving diversity of age/size classes
Stock rebuilding requires restoration of age structure, not just numbers

Bottom line: Assessing only total abundance without understanding population structure is like checking body weight without measuring vital signs—you may miss critical health problems until it’s too late.

title: Practical on Length-weight measurements
text:
The length-weight relationship (LWR) remains a fundamental tool in fisheries science for estimating biomass, assessing fish health, and understanding growth patterns. This relationship is mathematically defined by the power law equation:
\[
W = a \times L^b
\]
Where:

 W  = weight of the fish (in grams),
 L  = length of the fish (in centimeters),

text:
The length-weight relationship (LWR) remains a fundamental tool in fisheries science for estimating biomass, assessing fish health, and understanding growth patterns. This relationship is mathematically defined by the power law equation:
\[
W = a \times L^b
\]
Where:

 W  = weight of the fish (in grams),
 L  = length of the fish (in centimeters),
 a  = intercept (a coefficient related to the condition factor of the fish),
 b  = slope (an exponent indicating the type of growth).

For easier statistical analysis, the equation is typically converted to a linear form using logarithms:
\[
Log(W) = Log(a) + b \times Log(L)
\]

title: Practical on Length-weight measurements
section: Growth Patterns Based on the Exponent ‘b’
text:
Growth Patterns Based on the Exponent ‘b’
The exponent b in the length-weight relationship provides insights into the growth patterns of fish. 
The value of b typically ranges between 2.5 and 3.5 in natural environments.

Isometric Growth (b=3): The fish maintains its shape as it grows, with weight increasing in proportion to the cube of its length.
Positive Allometric Growth (b>3): The fish becomes “plumper” or heavier as it increases in length.
Negative Allometric Growth (b<3): The fish becomes “slimmer” or more elongated as it grows.

title: Glossary
text:
Abundance Index A relative measure of population size derived from survey data or fishery catch-per-unit-effort. Does not provide absolute population size but indicates trends over time.
Age Determination The process of estimating fish age through methods such as otolith reading, scale reading, or vertebral section examination.
Age-Structured Model A stock assessment model that divides the population into age classes and projects each class forward through time, accounting for growth, mortality, and reproduction.




Bycatch Fish species or individuals caught incidentally while targeting other species. Often discarded or of lower commercial value.
Biomass Total weight of all fish in a population or stock at a given time.




Catchability (q) The proportion of the population in an area that is caught per unit of fishing effort. Ranges from 0 to 1.
Catch-per-Unit-Effort (CPUE) Total catch divided by total fishing effort. Used as an index of fish abundance (CPUE = q × Abundance).
Catch Assessment Survey (CAS) A systematic survey designed to estimate total catch from a fishery based on sampling landing sites or fishing effort and using raising factors.
Coefficient of Variation (CV) Standard deviation expressed as a percentage of the mean. Used to measure relative variability in estimates.




Discard Fish that are caught but returned to the sea, either dead or alive. Often occurs when catch regulations are exceeded or fish have low market value.
Discardability The proportion of catch that is discarded.




Effort A measure of fishing intensity, including number of vessels, fishing time, gear quantity, or other measures of fishing activity.
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) A zone extending 200 nautical miles from a country’s coastline where the country has exclusive rights to exploit natural resources.




Fishery-Dependent Data Data collected directly from the fishing process itself, including landing records, onboard observer data, and fisher reports.
Fishery-Independent Data Data collected through research activities independent of the fishing process, such as research surveys and tagging experiments.
Fecundity The number of eggs produced by a female fish, often related to body size.
Frame Survey A census-based survey that collects data on all fishing vessels, gear, and landing sites to establish a sampling frame and generate raising factors.




Gear Selectivity The property of fishing gear to catch fish of certain sizes more readily than others. Typically expressed as a selectivity curve.
Gonad The reproductive organ in fish. Examination of gonad development determines maturity status.




Harvest Rate The proportion of the population removed by fishing in a given time period (usually annually).




Landing Records Official records of fish catch that are landed and sold at ports. The most common source of fishery-dependent data.
Length-Weight Relationship A mathematical relationship between fish length and weight, typically expressed as W = aL^b.




Maturity Staging Classification of fish gonad development (immature, maturing, mature, spent) to determine reproductive status.
Mortality The rate at which fish are lost from a population. Includes natural mortality, fishing mortality, and other causes.




Onboard Observer A government personnel who rides aboard fishing vessels to collect catch, bycatch, discard, and other data.
Otolith The ear bone of fish used for age determination. Growth rings (annuli) indicate age similar to tree rings.




Portside Sampling Collection of biological data (length, age, sex, maturity) from a sample of catch at landing sites.
Population Parameter A characteristic of the population such as abundance, growth rate, mortality rate, or reproduction rate.




Raising Factor A multiplier used to expand sample data to population estimates. Calculated as the ratio of population size to sample size.
Recruitment The addition of new, juvenile fish to the exploitable population through reproduction and growth.
Reference Point A target or limit value for a population parameter (e.g., biomass, harvest rate) used in fisheries management.




Sampling Frame A complete listing of all units (e.g., vessels, landing sites) in a population from which a sample is drawn.
Selectivity Curve A mathematical function describing how gear selectivity varies with fish size.
Sexual Maturity The developmental stage when fish become capable of reproduction.
Standardization A statistical process to adjust catch-per-unit-effort data for effects of non-biological factors (vessel characteristics, season, environmental conditions) to obtain a more accurate abundance index.
Stock A population of fish of the same species in a geographic area that shares similar ecological characteristics and is managed as a unit.
Stock Assessment An evaluation of the current status and trends of a fish stock using collected data and mathematical models.
Surplus Production The amount of biomass growth available for sustainable harvest from a population.




Vessel Monitoring System (VMS) Electronic device that automatically records and transmits the location of a fishing vessel, used for monitoring fishing effort and spatial distribution.
Von Bertalanffy Growth Equation The standard mathematical model for describing fish growth: L(t) = L∞(1 - e^(-K(t-t0)))




Year Class All fish born during the same breeding season or calendar year.
